title: The Convergence Point Where Reaching Ends

features.name: the vanishing point where rows converge
features.desc-on-touch: All the cottages, all the rows, all the paths—they meet here. The perspective is perfect: distance becomes a point so small you can almost touch it. But touching it would destroy the distance. The convergence point teaches: reaching ends when you understand that reaching is the only motion that matt

features.name: children's names carved in the convergence stone
features.desc-on-touch: They sorted the children. Now you see their names on the marker stone at this point: a roster of who reached here, who learned the lesson. Some names are scratched deep; others are barely marks. The stone records the effort of reaching differently for each person.

features.name: distance made solid
features.desc-on-touch: You can measure the horizon here. The distance is not empty; it has weight, substance, a texture you can read. The convergence point has crystallized infinity into a thing you can hold in your palm—not metaphorically; the air itself feels substantial, dense with arriving-and-never-arriving.

features.name: the endless row where nothing ends
features.desc-on-touch: Behind you, the cottages continue forever—but that is not what you see when you stand here. Standing at the convergence, you are outside the row. You can see it all at once, compressed into a line, infinite and still. The row has learned that 'endless' and 'complete' might be the same thing.

features.name: hands teaching empty hands to reach
features.desc-on-touch: An older child shows a younger child how to reach toward the point. Not frantically, but with the knowledge that reaching is an end in itself. The gesture is so patient it looks like stillness. You watch the teaching of reaching-that-never-arrives.

inscription: the cottages learned to stay in rows while the children learned to reach beyond them

reverie.title: REVERIE — teaching reach
narr: You both stand among the cottages, watching
how the rows converge toward nothing.
She takes your hand—not to reach together,
but to teach you how reaching is done: open,
patient, knowing the distance will never close.
You learn: reaching is not about arriving.
